title: The Letter to Titus
subtitle: Pros Titon, “To Titus”
description: Paul’s short letter to Titus, his Gentile co-worker, left on the island of Crete to put the churches in order and appoint elders in every town. Brisk and practical, it sets out what an elder must be, warns against teachers who are “ruining whole households”, and shows how older and younger, men and women, slaves and citizens can make the teaching about God our Savior attractive. And twice it stops to say why: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people, and teaches us to live while we wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ; and God saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to Titus?
qa.answer: A short letter in the New Testament from the apostle Paul to Titus, his co-worker, whom he had left on Crete to set the young churches in order and appoint elders in every town (1:5). With 1 and 2 Timothy it is one of the three Pastoral Letters. It describes what an elder must be, warns against false teachers, gives instructions for believers of every age and station, and grounds them in two great summaries of the gospel (2:11–14; 3:4–7).

qa.question: Who was Titus, and who wrote the letter?
qa.answer: Titus was a Greek believer whom Paul took to Jerusalem as an uncircumcised Gentile convert (Galatians 2:1–3) and later sent to the church at Corinth, calling him “a partner of mine” (2 Corinthians 8:23). The letter names Paul as its author, and the church received it as his, written in the 60s AD after a mission on Crete not recorded in Acts. Many modern scholars think the Pastoral Letters were written by a follower of Paul after his death; many others defend Paul’s authorship.

qa.question: Does Titus 2:13 call Jesus God?
qa.answer: It speaks of “the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.” Because one article in the Greek governs both “God” and “Savior”, the phrase most naturally names one person, Jesus Christ, as our great God and Savior, and most translations, including this one, read it that way. Some read two persons, God the Father and Christ, since the letter elsewhere calls the Father “God our Savior”. Either way, the verse sets Christ’s coming in glory at the centre of Christian hope.

qa.question: What qualifications for elders does the Letter to Titus give?
qa.answer: An elder must be blameless, “the husband of one wife, with children who believe”, and a household in order (1:6). Paul calls the same leader an overseer, who manages God’s household, and says he must not be arrogant or quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent or greedy for money, but hospitable, self-controlled, upright, holy and disciplined, holding firmly to the trustworthy message so that he can encourage with sound teaching and correct those who oppose it (1:7–9). The list is close to 1 Timothy 3. Christians differ on what “the husband of one wife” requires: faithfulness in marriage, no polygamy, or no remarriage.

qa.question: What does “the washing of new birth” mean in Titus 3:5?
qa.answer: Paul says God saved us “not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy”, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us generously through Jesus Christ our Savior (3:5–6). The Greek word means “becoming again”, which older Bibles render “regeneration”. Many Christians see in the washing a reference to baptism; others a cleansing that baptism pictures. All agree that it is God’s work and not ours, and that its fruit is a people justified by his grace, heirs with the hope of eternal life, and devoted to doing good.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
